---
title: "Independent practice lab"
subtitle: "From a research question to a reproducible analysis and an honest interpretation"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you will learn"}
Bring together the skills from the book: **inspect** a dataset, **filter and aggregate** observations, **reshape** a table, **describe and visualize distributions**, **analyze change over time**, **check a join**, and **explain the limits of your conclusions**. An optional research extension practices **OLS, logistic regression, and regression tables** using fictional data.
:::

## Your first mini research project

Throughout these exercises, we have learned separate skills. In this lab, you will put them together to answer a coherent research question, rather than simply reproduce one command at a time.

> **Research question:** How are recorded refugee stocks distributed across destinations in 2022, and how did the recorded stocks of Germany, France, and Spain change between 2015 and 2022?

You will use `refugees::population`, the same UNHCR dataset introduced earlier. We deliberately choose **end-of-year stocks**, not asylum applications or annual arrivals. The exercise is about **description and measurement**, not about assessing the effectiveness of refugee law or identifying the causes of a country's policies.

Later, you will use a **fictional asylum-decisions dataset** to practice recognition and protection rates. The optional extensions revisit joins and regression, drawing on the more advanced chapters.

::: {.callout-important title="Keep measurement and programming separate"}
A command can be correct R code but answer the wrong research question. For every calculation, state **what each row represents, which people are counted, the year, and the denominator (if any)**. If you are unsure, describe the result as a *reported* or *recorded* quantity rather than making claims about all people or all decisions.
:::

### Choose your route

| Route | Sections | Approximate time | Suitable for |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **Core lab** | A–F | 2.5–3.5 hours | Everyone completing the introductory chapters |
| **Research extension** | G–I | 1.5–2.5 additional hours | Colleagues comfortable with joins and regression |

Times are indicative, not deadlines. You may work over several sessions. It is fine to consult the previous sections, documentation, and your notes—but **explain each command you use**.

## Before you start: your files and workflow

Work inside an RStudio project, not directly in the Console. Your project should eventually look something like this:

```text
refugee-lab/
├── refugee-lab.Rproj
├── refugee-exploration.R
├── data/
│   └── toy_asylum_decisions.csv
├── figures/
│   ├── top-destinations-2022.png
│   ├── distribution-2022.png
│   └── refugee-trends-2015-2022.png
└── report.qmd            # optional, but recommended
```

If you are working within the Quarto project itself, the fictional decisions file is already at `data/toy_asylum_decisions.csv`. If you create a **separate RStudio project**, copy that file into its `data/` folder. Do not download or fabricate UNHCR data manually: load the `refugees` package as in earlier sections

You can also use the [starter R script](exercises/refugee-capstone-starter.R). It contains section headings, package-loading commands, and spaces for your solutions. The starter is **not a finished analysis**.

::: {.callout-tip title="A useful habit"}
At the beginning of your script, add a short header with the research question, the author, the date, and the data source. Put `library()` commands near the top. Install packages once in the **Console**, not every time the script runs.
:::

## Part A — Set up, inspect, and define an observation

**Goal:** Make sure you understand your starting table *before* calculating any statistics.

1. Create a project and save a script called `refugee-exploration.R`.
2. Load `refugees`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `ggplot2`, and `readr` (install any missing packages separately in the Console).
3. Save `refugees::population` as an object called `pop`.
4. Run `head()`, `glimpse()`, `names()`, `nrow()`, and `ncol()` on `pop`. What does each command tell you?
5. Select the columns `year`, `coo_iso`, `coo_name`, `coa_iso`, `coa_name`, `refugees`, and `asylum_seekers` and inspect a few rows.
6. **Write one sentence** defining a row of the original table. Is one row a person, a country, a country-year, or something more specific?
7. Run `packageVersion("refugees")` and record the result. Why might a colleague obtain different descriptive totals with an updated data release?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Need a starting point?"}

The following commands show how to begin; they **do not** complete the tasks above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(refugees)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

pop <- refugees::population

glimpse(pop)
packageVersion("refugees")
```
:::


:::

**Checkpoint A:** You can explain the difference between **origin** and **destination** (`coo` versus `coa`) and between a **refugee stock** and the number of applications received during a year.

## Part B — Create a country-level table and describe its distribution

**Goal:** Transform origin–destination records into a destination-level table for **2022**, and investigate what a *typical* destination looks like.

1. Filter `pop` to `year == 2022`. Keep records with a non-missing destination code.
2. Use `group_by(coa_iso, coa_name)` and `summarise()` to create `hosts_2022`, with one row per recorded destination entity and its **sum of `refugees` across origins**.
3. Inspect the number of origin records contributing to each destination. Check whether any source counts are missing. What happens when you use `sum(..., na.rm = TRUE)` on a group where *every* value is `NA`?
4. Verify the new unit of analysis: how many rows are there, and do destination codes repeat?
5. Calculate the **mean**, **median**, **standard deviation**, **minimum**, **maximum**, **25th percentile**, and **75th percentile** of destination-level stocks. Report them as **people** or in **millions**.
6. Create a ranking of the ten largest included destinations.
7. Calculate the **share of the included destination total** represented by the five largest destinations. Write the numerator and denominator in words.
8. Compare mean and median. Does the pattern suggest a **right-skewed distribution**? What would help you check this visually?

::: {.callout-warning title="Missing is not zero"}
A common beginner shortcut is `sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE)`. It excludes missing cells, but returns zero if **all** values in the group are missing. When that could happen, check missingness explicitly and preserve an unknown total rather than silently reporting zero. Also remember that ISO-like codes or labels can refer to special reporting entities; an automatic ranking is not yet a publication-ready country comparison.
:::

**Checkpoint B:** Write three short sentences: the meaning of your **mean**, the meaning of your **median**, and precisely **what population is in your top-five-share denominator**.

## Part C — Tell the story with several visualizations

**Goal:** Use graphs to understand a distribution, not simply decorate a report. Save **at least three** figures.

**Figure 1 — Who are the largest reported destinations?** Use `ggplot()` with `geom_col()` to plot the ten largest destinations in 2022. Make the bars horizontal, order them by the number of refugees, and label the axis in millions. State the year, category, and source in the title/caption. Explain why `geom_col()` is appropriate instead of the default `geom_bar()`.

**Figure 2 — What does the distribution look like?** Use `geom_histogram()` for **all included destination-level observations**. Try 10, 25, and 40 bins. Which features remain stable? Which change with the choice of bins? Mark the mean and median with vertical lines or explain where they fall.

**Figure 3 — Are there unusually large observations?** Make a boxplot of destination-level stocks. Explain the median, the middle 50%, and the points identified by the boxplot rule. Why is an outlier **not necessarily a data error**?

**Figure 4 — Optional:** Reproduce the histogram or boxplot using a logarithmic scale **only for strictly positive stocks**. Explain what the log scale makes easier to see, what it changes visually, and which observations you excluded.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Graph-building hints"}

- Use `arrange(desc(...))` and `slice_head(n = 10)` or `slice_max()` to choose the ten largest values.
- `reorder(country, value)` controls category ordering on a plot.
- A histogram counts **destinations in bins**; a bar chart of totals depicts **people by destination**.
- `geom_vline(xintercept = ...)` adds a vertical reference line.
- Use `ggsave("figures/your-figure.png", width = 8, height = 5)` to export a figure.

:::

**Checkpoint C:** Write an accurate caption for each figure. Compare what **a bar chart**, **a histogram**, and **a boxplot** can tell us. Does right-skewness mean that most refugees live in small destinations? Be careful: a distribution over *destination units* and a distribution over *people* answer different questions.

## Part D — Follow stocks through time and reshape the data

**Goal:** Compare **absolute levels**, **relative growth**, and **annual changes** for Germany, France, and Spain over 2015–2022.

1. Construct `series` with one row for each **destination–year**, using `coa_iso %in% c("DEU", "FRA", "ESP")`, `year >= 2015`, and `year <= 2022`. Aggregate `refugees` over origins **within each destination–year**.
2. Make a **line chart** of the three stock series. Label the y-axis in millions, and do not call the values *arrivals*.
3. Make a **faceted chart** with one panel for each destination. What is gained or lost when each facet has its own y-axis scale?
4. Create an **indexed series**, setting each destination's 2015 value equal to 100. Why can this make growth trajectories easier to compare than levels alone?
5. Sort by destination and year. Use `lag()` to calculate the **absolute annual change** and **percentage annual change**. Check that adjacent rows really correspond to adjacent years; if a year is missing, a lag is not automatically a one-year change.
6. Plot either the absolute changes or percentage changes. Explain why the country with the largest numerical increase need not have the largest percentage increase.
7. Practice **reshaping**: use `pivot_wider()` to make one column per year for a small period such as 2020–2022; then use `pivot_longer()` to return to the destination–year format. Check that the values are preserved.

Useful formulas:

$$
\text{Absolute change}_{t}=S_t-S_{t-1},\qquad
\text{Percentage change}_{t}=100\left(\frac{S_t}{S_{t-1}}-1\right).
$$

$$
\text{Index}_{t}=100\times\frac{S_t}{S_{2015}}.
$$

When a denominator is zero or missing, ordinary percentage growth is not defined. Do **not** substitute 0%. Consider how missing years or changes in the reported series affect interpretation.

::: {.callout-important title="The key substantive distinction"}
A change in an **end-of-year refugee stock** is not a count of new arrivals, and it cannot by itself tell us what caused the change. Returns, deaths, births, legal status changes, registration, reporting, and statistical revisions may all contribute to changes in the recorded stock.
:::

**Checkpoint D:** Write a short paragraph distinguishing **what the graphs show**, **what you hypothesize**, and **what additional evidence would be needed** to evaluate the hypothesis.

## Part E — Calculate a rate with a defensible denominator

**Goal:** Use the fictional dataset from the asylum-decisions chapter to see why a percentage needs a well-defined numerator and denominator.

1. Load `data/toy_asylum_decisions.csv` using `readr::read_csv()`.
2. Inspect the column names. The five destinations and all counts are **fictional**.
3. Compute **substantive decisions** as `recognized + other_protection + rejected`.
4. Calculate **refugee recognition rate** and **total protection rate** for each fictional destination, as percentages of *substantive decisions*.
5. Make one graph comparing the two rates across the five destinations (use `pivot_longer()` if useful).
6. Check **Albia** by hand. Its refugee recognition rate should be **45%**, and its total protection rate should be **60%**.
7. Explain why `closed` is not included in these **specific** substantive-outcome denominators. Is a rate among this year's substantive decisions the probability that an application lodged this year will eventually be recognized?

$$
\text{Refugee recognition rate}=100\times
\frac{\text{Recognized}}{\text{Recognized}+\text{Other protection}+\text{Rejected}}
$$

$$
\text{Total protection rate}=100\times
\frac{\text{Recognized}+\text{Other protection}}{\text{Recognized}+\text{Other protection}+\text{Rejected}}.
$$

**Checkpoint E:** Explain the difference between **percentage** and **percentage points**. For example, is the difference between 45% and 60% **15 percentage points** or **15 percent**?

## Part F — Make a join, but do not invent an indicator

**Goal:** Practice joining real UNHCR tables without accidentally treating incompatible application records as a comparable country ranking.

1. Inspect the column names in `refugees::asylum_applications`. Use `count(app_type, app_pc, sort = TRUE)` to identify the reported application types and cases/persons units.
2. For **2022**, create an `app_coverage` table with one row per nonmissing `coa_iso` and a count of **source rows with application records** (not a sum of people or claims).
3. `left_join()` this coverage table to `hosts_2022` by destination code.
4. Check whether both tables have **unique destination keys** before the join. How many stock destinations have no matching application-reporting row?
5. Use `anti_join()` to list the unmatched keys. Explain why a missing match should not automatically become zero applications.
6. **Optional:** Repeat across 2015–2022, joining on **both** `coa_iso` and `year`. Why is joining by destination alone no longer safe?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Join-checking hints"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Checking uniqueness does not require a join
hosts_2022 |>
  count(coa_iso) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# Example syntax for a composite key
# left_join(table_one, table_two, by = c("coa_iso", "year"))
```
:::


Think carefully about the difference between `n()` (number of rows) and `sum(applied)` (a quantity whose unit and procedural coverage you would need to harmonize).

:::

::: {.callout-warning title="A successful join is not a valid recognition measure"}
A match on destination and year does **not** mean that application records, decision records, and population stocks cover the same people. Application types, first versus repeated claims, appeal levels, cases versus persons, coverage, and the time lag between filing and decisions matter. Do not divide annual decisions by annual applications and label the result the individual's chance of protection.
:::

**Checkpoint F:** Write two reasons why an exact join can still yield a misleading substantive comparison.

## Research extension — Work with regression results

The remaining parts build on the inference section. They use **fictional data only**, so you can learn regression syntax and interpretation without implying that UNHCR aggregate data identify causal effects. Complete these if you have finished the core lab or want extra practice.

## Part G — Correlation, OLS, and an interpretable regression table

**Research prompt:** In a fictional set of administrative jurisdictions, are staffing levels associated with average processing duration? **Core-lab participants can skip Parts G–H and continue directly to Part I.**

First, generate the example data. You can paste this block into your script and run it as written; **every observation is invented**.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)

n_jurisdictions <- 160

jurisdictions <- tibble(
  jurisdiction = sprintf("J%03d", seq_len(n_jurisdictions)),
  complexity = runif(n_jurisdictions, min = 0, max = 1),
  resources = rnorm(n_jurisdictions)
) |>
  mutate(
    staff_per_100 = pmax(
      1.5,
      6 + 1.4 * resources - 1.8 * complexity +
        rnorm(n_jurisdictions, sd = 1)
    ),
    processing_months = pmax(
      0.5,
      16 - 0.7 * staff_per_100 + 4 * complexity -
        0.6 * resources + rnorm(n_jurisdictions, sd = 1.8)
    )
  )
```
:::


1. Plot staffing (`staff_per_100`) against processing duration (`processing_months`) and calculate their Pearson correlation using `cor()`.
2. Estimate **Model 1**, an OLS regression of processing duration on staffing using `lm()`.
3. Estimate **Model 2**, adding `complexity` and `resources`.
4. Inspect `summary()`, `coef()`, `confint()`, `fitted()`, and `residuals()` for at least one model.
5. Explain the staffing coefficient in **months per additional staff member per 100 pending cases**. Compare Models 1 and 2 without claiming a causal effect.
6. Identify the intercept, slope, standard error, 95% confidence interval, p-value, number of observations, and $R^2$. Distinguish **precision** from **substantive importance**.
7. Create a regression table with `stargazer::stargazer()` or `modelsummary::modelsummary()`. State clearly what is reported in parentheses and which variables are included.
8. Use `broom::tidy()` to extract a tidy coefficient table, including confidence intervals. Make a coefficient plot if you want a graphical extension.

::: {.callout-tip title="Reading a regression table"}
Do not just say that the coefficient is “significant.” Say **which outcome is being modeled, the unit of the coefficient, whether it is positive or negative, how uncertain the estimate is, and what comparison the model makes**. A statistically precise estimate can be substantively small, and observational associations are not necessarily causal.
:::

### Optional: logarithms

Estimate a model with `log(processing_months)` as the outcome (the generated durations are positive). Compare the unit interpretation of its staffing coefficient with the coefficient in the level model. For a log-outcome model, a one-unit increase in a regressor corresponds to an **exact** fitted multiplicative change of $e^{\beta}$ (or $100(e^{\beta}-1)\%$), conditional on the model; the common $100\beta\%$ rule is an approximation for small coefficients. Explain why this is **not** an odds ratio.

## Part H — Logistic regression, odds ratios, and predicted probabilities

**Research prompt:** In fictional application-level data, how is legal representation associated with an invented binary recognition outcome, conditional on selected variables?

Create this separate **fictional** application-level dataset (no UNHCR claim-level data are involved):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2027)

n_applications <- 650

claims <- tibble(
  claim_id = seq_len(n_applications),
  evidence_index = rnorm(n_applications),
  represented = rbinom(n_applications, size = 1, prob = 0.45),
  origin_group = factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C"),
                               n_applications, replace = TRUE))
) |>
  mutate(
    p_recognized = plogis(
      -0.8 + 0.75 * evidence_index + 0.55 * represented +
        if_else(origin_group == "B", -0.4, 0) +
        if_else(origin_group == "C", 0.35, 0)
    ),
    recognized = rbinom(n(), size = 1, prob = p_recognized)
  )
```
:::


1. Verify that `recognized` takes only values 0 and 1. Calculate the **observed proportion recognized**.
2. Estimate `glm(recognized ~ represented + evidence_index + origin_group, data = claims, family = binomial(link = "logit"))`.
3. Interpret the coefficient for `represented` as a difference in **log-odds**, then use `exp(coef(model))` to express it as an **odds ratio**.
4. Use `predict(model, newdata = ..., type = "response")` for two otherwise identical hypothetical profiles that differ only in `represented`. State the **difference in predicted probabilities in percentage points**.
5. Explain why an odds ratio of 2 does **not** mean that the predicted probability doubles or that it increases by 100 percentage points.
6. Make a second regression table or a tidy odds-ratio table with 95% confidence intervals. Label the coefficient scale correctly.

::: {.callout-warning title="Fictional associations, not real causal claims"}
The simulation makes relationships deliberately visible. In real refugee-status determination data, access to representation, case characteristics, procedural stages, and selection mechanisms may be correlated. A logistic regression that controls for a few observed variables does **not** automatically estimate the causal impact of representation on protection outcomes.
:::




## Self-assessment: can you explain your work?

| Before submitting, check that… | Not yet | Almost | Yes |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| My script runs in a clean R session | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I recorded the data source and package version | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I can explain the original and derived units of observation | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I know the difference between `NA` and a recorded zero | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I can distinguish a total, a mean, a median, and a share | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I inspected the distribution and explained possible skewness | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My charts have clear axes, units, dates, and captions | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I can distinguish absolute change, percentage change, and an index | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I can reshape wide and long data without changing what the rows mean | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My joined tables have defensible, checked keys | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I never interpreted stock changes as arrivals | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My recognition/protection rates use a stated denominator | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| *(Extension)* I can interpret OLS coefficients with units and uncertainty | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| *(Extension)* I can distinguish log-odds, odds ratios, and probabilities | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My conclusions do not exceed what the data and design support | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

::: {.callout-tip title="The real test"}
The goal is **not** to produce the largest number of graphs or the fanciest regression table. It is to be able to hand someone your files and explain **where every number came from, what it measures, and why your interpretation is justified**.
:::

For reminders about R terminology, consult the [glossary](glossary.qmd) and [resources](resources.qmd). Revisit the chapters on [data transformation](03-wrangling.qmd), [visualization](05-visualization.qmd), [time trends](06-time-trends.qmd), [applications and decisions](07-applications-decisions.qmd), [joins](08-comparing-data.qmd), and [inference](09-inference.qmd) as needed.
